passages.text: But someone will say, “If he has a form, he also has a shape and is in a place. If he is in a place and contained by it as something lesser, how is he great above all? And how can he be everywhere while having a shape?” To the person saying this, one can first say: those around Simon persuade people to believe such thoughts about him; but we know to be true the things attested by our Lord Jesus Christ. Proofs that this is so must be supplied to you, not on the basis of a command. But first I will speak about place and God. Place is what does not exist, whereas God is what exists; and what does not exist cannot be compared with what exists. For how can place have existence, unless it is a second region, such as heaven, earth, water, air, or any other body, which would also fill the void there? It is called void for this reason: because it is nothing. Nothing is a more suitable name for it. For what is the so-called void—some sort of vessel that contains nothing? Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, place is that in which the void itself is, if indeed it is a vessel. For what exists must necessarily be in what is nothing. This is what I mean by what does not exist, which some call place: it is nothing. How can what is nothing be compared with what exists, except as opposites, so that what exists is not called place, but what does not exist is? But even if it is something, although many examples press to come forth from me as proof, I wish to use just one, to show that what contains is not invariably stronger than what is contained. The sun is a circular shape and is wholly contained by air, but it illuminates the air, heats it, and cuts through it. When the sun is absent from it, the air is enveloped in darkness, and wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying. But at the sun’s rising it is illuminated again, and wherever it is warmed by the sun it is also adorned with greater beauty. The sun does these things by its presence, although its substance is bounded. What, then, still prevents God, as the maker and master of this and all things, while he himself has shape, form, and beauty, from having the presence proceeding from him extended infinitely?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀληθεῖς γινώσκομεν τὰς μαρτυρουμένας
lexical_decisions.chosen: we know to be true the things attested
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine plural has no expressed noun; things or statements attested expresses the ellipsis without adding an extra source claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μὲν ὂν μὴ ᾖ, τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν τόπος λέγηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: what exists is not called place, but what does not exist is
lexical_decisions.rationale: Understands place from the second clause as the predicate to the first, not an assertion that what exists ceases to exist.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied wording says bright, not dark. The resulting physical description is puzzling, but the main text preserves that printed adjective rather than silently emending it to fit the argument. Its referent is understood as a part of the air.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μετουσίαν ἀπείρως ἐκτεταμένην ἔχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: from having the presence proceeding from him extended infinitely
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετουσία can be presence, participation, or communicated influence. Presence preserves the analogy with the bounded sun’s effects without adding a second bodily substance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃ ἂν καὶ αὐτοῦ πληροῦν τὸ κενόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: which would also fill the void there
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes αὐτοῦ locatively, there, referring to the discussed place or region. It is not nominative emphatic αὐτό, itself. A genitive alternative is which would also fill its void, with the precise possessive referent drawn from the surrounding body/region discussion; no replacement Greek is adopted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τί οὖν ἔτι κωλύει τὸν θεὸν ὡς τούτου καὶ πάντων δημιουργὸν καὶ δεσπότην ὄντα, αὐτὸν μὲν ἐν σχήματι καὶ μορφῇ καὶ κάλλει ὄντα, τὴν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μετουσίαν ἀπείρως ἐκτεταμένην ἔχειν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: What, then, still prevents God, as the maker and master of this and all things, while he himself has shape, form, and beauty, from having the presence proceeding from him extended infinitely?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participial descriptions present God as maker/master and as himself being in shape, form, and beauty. The infinitive governed by prevents concerns his having the presence proceeding from him infinitely extended. The revised question preserves that grammatical focus rather than making the shape itself the prevented action and the extension merely circumstantial.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ κατὰ κέλευσιν τὰς ἀποδείξεις ὑμῖν τοῦ οὕτως ἔχειν ἀνάγκη παρέχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Proofs that this is so must be supplied to you, not on the basis of a command.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text gives οὐ narrow scope over κατὰ κέλευσιν, leaving the obligation ἀνάγκη παρέχειν affirmative. The immediate placement of the negative before the command phrase favors this source-transparent scope, and the following developed proofs fit an obligation to supply demonstration rather than an appeal to command. A materially different broad scope denies obligation on command: We are not obliged to provide you at a command with proofs that things are so. The latter is a possible contextual construal, but the main text does not insert a negative before ἀνάγκη or claim the two scopes are equivalent. The source does not identify whose command is meant.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν αὐτὸ τὸ σκεῦος κενὸν ὂν οὐκ αὐτό ἐστι τόπος, ἀλλ’ ἐν ᾧ ἐστὶν αὐτὸ τὸ κενόν, εἴπερ σκεῦός ἐστιν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, place is that in which the void itself is, if indeed it is a vessel.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text renders substantival αὐτὸ τὸ κενόν as the void itself, preserving the recurring κενόν earlier called void and tested hypothetically as a vessel. If indeed it is a vessel retains that conditional uncertainty rather than affirming that the void is a physical container. A contextual ellipsis can instead supply vessel from the preceding σκεῦος: Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, if it is a vessel, place is that in which the empty vessel itself is. The final vessel proviso supports that alternative, but the repeated substantive void is more source-transparent and no unprinted second vessel noun is required. The precise conditional referent remains open between the hypothesized void/container and the vessel already under discussion.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
source_issues.issue: The wording associates becoming bright with cooling, which is puzzling in this analogy. Bright is nevertheless what the supplied text says; no emendation to dark has been made.
